message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel, data‑intensive tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each highly optimized for complex control flow, low latency, and large caches. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores, optimized for throughput, with many registers and small caches per core. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) with sophisticated branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution, and large pipelines. | Simpler instruction set (often SIMD), focused on executing the same operation on many data elements simultaneously. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, sophisticated prefetchers. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on massive shared memory bandwidth and specialized memory (e.g., GDDR5/6). |
| **Parallelism** | Limited parallelism – a few threads per core, heavy emphasis on single‑thread performance. | Massive data‑parallelism – thousands of lightweight threads running concurrently. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control‑heavy tasks, branching logic, I/O, operating system services. | Data‑parallel tasks: matrix multiplication, convolution, image/video processing, deep‑learning inference/training. |
| **Power & Heat** | Designed for low power consumption per core, efficient at handling diverse workloads. | Higher power density; GPUs can consume several hundred watts under full load. |
| **Programming Model** | Traditional sequential programming, multithreading via OS schedulers. | Parallel programming models like CUDA, OpenCL, or SYCL; requires explicit thread management and memory transfers. |

In short, CPUs excel at tasks that require strong single‑thread performance and complex decision making, while GPUs shine when you need to perform the same operation on many data items in parallel. That’s why modern systems often combine both: the CPU handles general control flow, and the GPU accelerates compute‑heavy kernels.
